Invariant expansion of the 30-band 𝒌⋅𝒑\bm{k}\!\dotproduct\!\bm{p} model and its parameters for III-V compounds

Krzysztof Gawarecki Email: Krzysztof.Gawarecki@pwr.edu.pl Affiliation: Department of Theoretical Physics, Wrocław University of Science and Technology, Wybrzeże Wyspiańskiego 27, 50-370 Wrocław, Poland    Paweł Scharoch Affiliation: Department of Semiconductor Materials Engineering, Wrocław University of Science and Technology, Wybrzeże Wyspiańskiego 27, 50-370 Wrocław, Poland    Michał Wiśniewski Affiliation: Department of Experimental Physics, Wrocław University of Science and Technology, Wybrzeże Wyspiańskiego 27, 50-370 Wrocław, Poland    Jakub Ziembicki Affiliation: Department of Semiconductor Materials Engineering, Wrocław University of Science and Technology, Wybrzeże Wyspiańskiego 27, 50-370 Wrocław, Poland    Herbert S. Mączko Affiliation: Department of Semiconductor Materials Engineering, Wrocław University of Science and Technology, Wybrzeże Wyspiańskiego 27, 50-370 Wrocław, Poland    Marta Gładysiewicz Affiliation: Department of Experimental Physics, Wrocław University of Science and Technology, Wybrzeże Wyspiańskiego 27, 50-370 Wrocław, Poland    Robert Kudrawiec Affiliation: Department of Semiconductor Materials Engineering, Wrocław University of Science and Technology, Wybrzeże Wyspiańskiego 27, 50-370 Wrocław, Poland
Abstract

In this work we derive a ready-to-use symmetry invariant expansion of the full-zone 3030-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p Hamiltonian for the TdT_{d} point group. In order to find respective parameters, the band structures of III-V materials were calculated within a state-of-the-art Density Functional Theory (DFT) approach and used next as targets to adjust the k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p bands. A satisfactory agreement of the k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p model with the DFT band structures, for all the tested zinc blende III-V semiconductors, has been achieved. Values of many of the parameters have not been known so far. We also compare the fitted k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p parameters with the values calculated using momentum matrix elements obtained directly from the DFT.

I Introduction

Zinc blende III-V semiconductors are key materials in modern optoelectronic devices including light emitting diodes (LED) and laser diodes (LDs) [1, 2, 3]. The active part of the current LEDs and LDs are usually quantum wells (QW) or quantum dots (QD). Their size and content can be controlled precisely while growing with the use of the molecular beam epitaxy or the organometallic chemical vapor deposition methods [4, 5, 6, 7]. A proper design of the structures in terms of the size and the content allows for an effective optimization of desired devices. For this purpose accurate band structure computations within efficient approaches are needed. A widely used class of the theoretical methods involves multiband k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p models with the envelope function approximation [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16]. However, some of their parameters are not well established for all the III-V semiconductors, especially when high-number-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p models are considered.

An accurate description of the first conduction bands across the entire Brillouin Zone (BZ) is of fundamental importance for quantitatively correct description of carrier transport phenomena [17], direct and indirect absorption calculations [18], optical gain calculations [19], etc. Therefore k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p models able to finely describe bands relevant for devices operation, with a complete set of material parameters, are desired. Furthermore, some of III-V semiconductor compounds that are not completely parametrized (such as boron pnictides) gained much attention recently in the field of optoelectronic devices [20, 21, 22, 23].

There are three popular high-number-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p models constructed with an aim to give an access to conduction bands across the entire BZ: 20-, 24-, and 30-band model. The 20-band model [24] is a direct extension of the 14-band model, giving a full access to the first conduction band with a satisfactory accuracy [25, 26]. However, it fails in description of the second conduction band, especially the 2nd L valley. The 24-band model is an extension of the 20-band model aiming at correcting the description of the valence bands and the two lowest conduction bands [27]. However, it still fails to finely reproduce the 2nd L valley and introduces a great number of parameters. These two models do not contain dd levels explicitly, which are essential for fine description of the two first conduction bands across the entire BZ. The 30-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p model typically allows for such an accurate description [28, 9], and with a smaller number of parameters than in the 20- or 24-band models. The 30-band model is self-contained, which means it does not include additional bands via perturbations. For this reason, this model is much easier to use than other high-number-band models. Therefore, this model is chosen in our work for a description of all currently important III-V semiconductor compounds. In contrast to simple k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p models, a lot of the parameters entering the high-number-band models are not directly accessible experimentally, so their determination is performed on the basis of fitting to band structures obtained within the state-of-the-art ab initio approaches. Also, schemes of obtaining the k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p parameters directly from the DFT calculations have been proposed [29].

Currently, the best known methods of determining the band structure are based on Density Functional Theory (DFT), either directly from Kohn-Sham equations with specially designed exchange-correlation (XC) potentials or within post-DFT methods (e.g. GW), in which Kohn-Sham solutions form a starting point [30]. However, the DFT methods are usually computationally heavy, and the results, like the wave functions, are given in big data files which are inconvenient for using in standard programs for electronic devices modeling, many of which had been created before ab initio methods were known. Therefore, the modeling usually exploits the k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p method in approximations sufficient to represent the electronic structure in required range of the BZ, and the DFT methods are applied to benchmark the approximations and provide the required parameters.

The multiband k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p models contain a number of parameters, whose values depend on atoms forming a given material. However, a general structure of a k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p model (including a non-zero pattern of its matrix elements) is determined by the symmetry. This universality is clearly visible in the theory of invariants, which allows to express the Hamiltonian by terms strictly connected to irreducible representations of a group describing the crystal symmetry [31, 32, 33]. Comparing to a straightforward formulation, where the Hamiltonian is written as a single matrix (which is less practical for the k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p models exceeding 88 bands), the invariant expansion offers more compact formulas with a clear structure connected to the symmetry. Also, due to well defined multiplication relations between sub-matrices forming blocks of the Hamiltonian, it is much more convenient (compared to the explicit-matrix formulation) to use perturbation techniques (the Löwdin partitioning) [34, 33, 35]. Invariant expansions for the eight- and fourteen-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p models for the TdT_{\mathrm{d}} point group were derived decades ago and well established [36, 32, 37, 33, 38]. Recently, in Ref. [39] authors used symmetry considerations to describe a way to construct any k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p model for any symmetry, and they give a very large database containing representation matrices (4 857 832 matrix blocks). However, its application is not straightforward. In consequence, although the properties of arbitrary-size models for the TdT_{\mathrm{d}} point group are known [40, 39], no convenient ready-to-use invariant-based formulation has been provided for the 3030-band model so far.

In this paper, we derive an explicit form of the Hamiltonian given in terms of the symmetry invariants. We also offer the parameters for a wide class of the III-V semiconductor materials found using the DFT (ab initio) reference electronic structures. The 30-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p model used here is usually sufficient to represent the electronic bands in the full BZ which is often necessary to properly describe the properties connected with the indirect electronic transitions. Finally, in the case of GaAs, we compare the fitted parameters to the values extracted directly from momentum matrix elements calculated in the DFT approach. We show a very good agreement for most of the parameters.

The paper is organized as follows. In Sec. II, we describe the 3030-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p model and its invariant expansion. In Sec. III, we present the DFT approach. Sec. IV is devoted to the parameters related to interband momentum matrix elements, which are further obtained directly from the DFT calculations. In Sec. V we briefly describe the k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p to DFT fitting procedure. In Sec. VI, we present examples of the k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p vs DFT band structures and the values of evaluated k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p parameters. In Sec. VII, we present an exemplary application of the model. Sec. VIII contains a summary. In Appendix A, one can find an explicit form of the Hamiltonian and matrices including a detailed description of derivation. Appendix B describes the reduction from the 30-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p to models with fewer bands. In Appendix C, the calculations related to the interband momentum matrix elements are presented. Finally, the complete set of the plotted band structures is given in the attached Supplementary Material [41].

II The 30 𝒌⋅𝒑\bm{k}\!\dotproduct\!\bm{p} model

In the approach of 3030-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p applied to materials of the diamond structure (the OhO_{\mathrm{h}} point group), the only non-vanishing interband momentum matrix elements are between the basis states of the different parity with respect to the inversion [9]. In the case of the zinc blende atomic structure, the inversion symmetry is broken [42] and number of additional parameters have to be introduced to the model [9]. However, their impact on the main spectral properties is usually weaker compared to the parameters non-vanishing for the diamond structure [38]. On the other hand, the bulk inversion asymmetry is important for spin-related properties (which is manifested via the Dresselhaus coupling) [43]. Since such effects in many applications are considered only in the vicinity of the Γ\Gamma point, near the fundamental band gap, we keep the parameters related to the inversion asymmetry in the part of the Hamiltonian corresponding to the 1414-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p model [37, 38] and neglect them otherwise [9] (except to one additional parameter in the valence band) .

The basis used in the considered model contains 3030 states which can be grouped according to the irreducible representations (Γ6\Gamma_{6}, Γ8\Gamma_{8} or Γ7\Gamma_{7}) of the Td\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{d}} point group [9]. Then, the Hamiltonian HH can be decomposed into the blocks

Hn​α​n′​α′=⟨𝚪n​α|H|𝚪n′​α′⟩,H_{n\alpha n^{\prime}\alpha^{\prime}}=\matrixelement{\bm{\Gamma}_{n\alpha}}{H}{\bm{\Gamma}_{n'\alpha'}}, (1)

where |𝚪n​α⟩\ket{\bm{\Gamma}_{n\alpha}} are pseudospinors with n=6,7,8n=6,7,8 denoting the representation and α=\alpha=’’w”, ’’v”, ’’c”, ’’u”, ’’t”, ’’d”, ’’q” labeling the band set. Size of matrices corresponding to each block are determined by dimΓn×dimΓn′\dim{\Gamma_{n}}\times\dim{\Gamma_{n^{\prime}}} [38]. Such blocks within the theory of invariants can be further expressed as combinations of irreducible tensor components [42, 38, 40].

The block-diagonal parts of the Hamiltonian can be written as

H6​α​6​α\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{6\alpha 6\alpha}} =(E~6​α+ℏ22​m0​k2)​𝕀2,\displaystyle=\quantity( \widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{6\alpha}} + \frac{\hbar^2}{2m_0} k^2 )\;\mathbb{I}_{2},
H8​α​8​α\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{8\alpha 8\alpha}} =(E~8​α+13​Δ~α​α+ℏ22​m0​k2)​𝕀4,\displaystyle=\quantity( \widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{8\alpha}} + \frac{1}{3} \widetilde{\Delta}_{\alpha\alpha} + \frac{\hbar^2}{2m_0} k^2 )\;\mathbb{I}_{4},
H7​α​7​α\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{7\alpha 7\alpha}} =(E~7​α−23​Δ~α​α+ℏ22​m0​k2)​𝕀2,\displaystyle=\quantity( \widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{7\alpha}} -\frac{2}{3} \widetilde{\Delta}_{\alpha\alpha}+ \frac{\hbar^2}{2m_0} k^2 )\;\mathbb{I}_{2},

where 𝕀n\mathbb{I}_{n} is the nn-th size identity matrix, E~m​α\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{m\alpha}} are bare energies at 𝒌=0\bm{k}=0 without the spin-orbit coupling, and m0m_{0} is the free electron mass. Finally, the diagonal corrections due to the spin-orbit coupling are introduced via the parameters Δ~α​α\widetilde{\Delta}_{\alpha\alpha}. As the energies E~m​α\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{m\alpha}} do not contain the spin-orbit part, it is convenient to label them using the single-group notation [9] (with the representations Γ1\Gamma_{1}, Γ5\Gamma_{5} and Γ3\Gamma_{3}), where E~6​α=E1​α\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{6\alpha}}={E}_{\mathrm{1\alpha}} and E~8​α=E~7​α=E5​α\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{8\alpha}}=\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{7\alpha}}={E}_{\mathrm{5\alpha}} (except α=\alpha=’’t”, where E~8​t=E3​t\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{8t}}={E}_{\mathrm{3t}}). The off-diagonal blocks of the Hamiltonian can be written in a general form

H6​α​8​β\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{6\alpha 8\beta}} =3​𝒫α​β​(Tx​kx+c.p.),\displaystyle=\sqrt{3}\mathcal{P}_{\alpha\beta}\quantity(T_x k_x + \cp),
H6​α​7​β\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{6\alpha 7\beta}} =−13​𝒫α​β​(σx​kx+c.p.),\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\mathcal{P}_{\alpha\beta}\quantity(\sigma_x k_x + \cp),
H8​α​8​β\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{8\alpha 8\beta}} =−23​𝒬α​β​({Jy,Jz}​kx+c.p.)\displaystyle=-\frac{2}{3}\mathcal{Q}_{\alpha\beta}\quantity(\{J_y,J_z\} k_x + \cp)
−30ℛα​β(Dxkx+c.p.)+13Δ~α​β𝕀4,\displaystyle\quad-\sqrt{30}\mathcal{R}_{\alpha\beta}(D_{x}k_{x}+{\mathrm{c.p.}})+\frac{1}{3}\widetilde{\Delta}_{\alpha\beta}\mathbb{I}_{4},
H8​α​7​β\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{8\alpha 7\beta}} =−2𝒬α​β(Ty​z†kx+c.p.)\displaystyle=-2\mathcal{Q}_{\alpha\beta}(T^{\dagger}_{yz}k_{x}+{\mathrm{c.p.}})
+6ℛα​β(Tx†kx+c.p.),\displaystyle\quad+\sqrt{6}\mathcal{R}_{\alpha\beta}(T^{\dagger}_{x}k_{x}+{\mathrm{c.p.}}),
H7​α​7​β\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{7\alpha 7\beta}} =−23​Δ~α​β​𝕀2,\displaystyle=-\frac{2}{3}\widetilde{\Delta}_{\alpha\beta}\mathbb{I}_{2},

where 𝒫α​β\mathcal{P}_{\alpha\beta}, 𝒬α​β\mathcal{Q}_{\alpha\beta}, and ℛα​β\mathcal{R}_{\alpha\beta} are parameters related to the interband momentum matrix elements, {A,B}=(A​B+B​A)/2\{A,B\}=(AB+BA)/2,  TiT_{i} are 2×42\times 4 matrices connecting different blocks, JiJ_{i} are 4×44\times 4 matrices related to the total angular momentum, Ti​j=Ti​Jj+Tj​JiT_{ij}=T_{i}J_{j}+T_{j}J_{i}, and DiD_{i} are 4×44\times 4 matrices. While we took the TiT_{i}, JiJ_{i}, and Ti​jT_{ij} from the literature [32], we derived the DiD_{i} matrices from the Wigner-Eckart theorem. The remaining blocks can be calculated from the hermitian conjugates Hn​α​m​β=Hm​β​n​α†H_{\mathrm{n\alpha m\beta}}=H^{\dagger}_{\mathrm{m\beta n\alpha}}. The calculation details, explicit definitions of the basis functions, matrices, and a ready-to-use form of the Hamiltonian are given in Appendix A. The invariant expansions of the Hamiltonian blocks, except to the ones involving ’’8t”, have the well known structure of the 1414-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p model [32, 38] with the same matrices TiT_{i}, JiJ_{i}, Ti​jT_{ij}; yet more parameters 𝒫α​β\mathcal{P}_{\alpha\beta}, 𝒬α​β\mathcal{Q}_{\alpha\beta} are needed.

In this work, to model the properties of the III-V materials, we keep the nonzero parameters enlisted in Table 1. As they impact on the bands of interest is expected to be rather subtle, we neglected off-diagonal spin-orbital parameters, except to Δ−\Delta^{-}.

III The ab initio approach

The main purpose of the DFT calculations in this work was to obtain high quality band structures which are needed as a reference to adjust the 3030-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p model. The method commonly regarded as the best one to represent the band structure is the DFT-based GW approach [44, 45]. However, in this work, we decided to use the HSE hybrid functional [46] which is known to provide, at a relatively low computational cost, an accurate description of electronic bands, as opposed to the standard LDA and GGA schemes, where the well known band gap problem is exhibited. Moreover, in the hybrid functional, the results may be further improved by fitting band gaps to the experimental ones with the μ\mu screening parameter [47]. For all the materials considered in this work (except BSb, as in this case, the experimental band gap is unknown) the value of the μ\mu parameter was rescaled to yield experimental band gaps [48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53]. The calculations of band structures were made with VASP code and PAW method [54, 55]. The Brillouin zone was sampled with the 11x11x11 grid and the energy cutoff was set to 600 eV.

The lattice parameters were optimized with the use of ABINIT [56] package together with the PAW method [57] and the Wu and Cohen GGA functional [58]. In Ref. [59], the authors showed that this functional yields very accurate lattice constants for this group of materials. Our calculations confirm this. The mean absolute deviation of their values with respect to experiment is about 0.3 %. In VASP, this particular functional is not implemented.

IV Extracting the 𝒌⋅𝒑\bm{k}\!\dotproduct\!\bm{p} model parameters directly from the DFT calculations

The parameters that enter the 30-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p Hamiltonian can be divided into three classes: the energies E~m​α\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{m\alpha}}, the spin-orbit coupling parameters Δ~α​β\widetilde{\Delta}_{\alpha\beta}, and the 𝒫α​β\mathcal{P}_{\alpha\beta}, 𝒬α​β\mathcal{Q}_{\alpha\beta}, ℛα​β\mathcal{R}_{\alpha\beta} which are related to interband momentum matrix elements. The E~m​α\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{m\alpha}} and the diagonal Δ~α​α\widetilde{\Delta}_{\alpha\alpha} are directly read from the DFT band energies at the Γ\Gamma point (which is an approximation, because the band energies at this point are also affected by the off-diagonal Δ~α​β\widetilde{\Delta}_{\alpha\beta} [60]). As the k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p basis is finite, the parameters related to interband momentum matrix elements need to be rescaled to obtain a better agreement to the target data. The 3030-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p contains a relatively large number of basis states, hence one can expect that bare 𝒫α​β\mathcal{P}_{\alpha\beta}, 𝒬α​β\mathcal{Q}_{\alpha\beta}, ℛα​β\mathcal{R}_{\alpha\beta}, calculated from the momentum matrix elements within the DFT approach, could give a reasonable approximation (or at least an initial value for further fitting).

While the parameters, which are given in the further part of the paper comes from the fitting, in the case of GaAs we also extract them directly from the DFT, and compare the values obtained in both methods. The VASP code contains a procedure, allowing to get the momentum matrix elements. With this, we calculate (pi)n​m=⟨Ψn|p^i|Ψm⟩(p_{i})_{nm}=\matrixelement{\Psi_n}{\hat{p}_{i}}{\Psi_m} for the states |Ψl⟩\ket{\Psi_l} at the Γ\Gamma point. To obtain the values of 𝒫α​β\mathcal{P}_{\alpha\beta}, 𝒬α​β\mathcal{Q}_{\alpha\beta}, and ℛα​β\mathcal{R}_{\alpha\beta}, one needs to extract the matrix elements between the basis states forming |Ψl⟩\ket{\Psi_l}. This, however, requires a caution due to degeneracies and complex phases. A detailed description of the applied procedure is presented in the Appendix C.

V Fitting the 30 band 𝒌⋅𝒑\bm{k}\!\dotproduct\!\bm{p} model parameters

The procedure of finding the 3030 band 𝒌⋅𝒑\bm{k}\cdot\bm{p} parameters, by adjusting the 𝒌⋅𝒑\bm{k}\cdot\bm{p} band structure to the DFT reference one, has been described in details in Ref. [19]. A central point of this procedure is a minimization of the objective function SS, defined as:

S=1N​∑i=1N(EDFT,i−E𝒌⋅𝒑,i)2,S=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(E_{\mathrm{DFT},i}-E_{\bm{k}\cdot\bm{p},i}\right)^{2}}, (2)

where EDFT,iE_{\mathrm{DFT},i} are energies of the DFT bands in a number of points in the BZ. In this work 4545 points in along high symmetry lines X−Γ−LX-\Gamma-L in the BZ have been chosen. The number of points is higher than in Ref. [19] because of the lower crystal symmetry (zinc blende vs diamond). The E𝒌⋅𝒑,iE_{\bm{k}\cdot\bm{p},i} are the corresponding energies of the fitted 𝒌⋅𝒑\bm{k}\cdot\bm{p} band structure. The summation runs over the 𝒌\bm{k} points in the BZ and over the bands, thus ii is a compound index. The function, after minimization, is also a measure of the accuracy of the fit, with zero representing a perfect match. The method of steepest descent has been used to find a minimum, which was previously shown to work very well for diamond structure materials [19]. The diagonal E~m​α\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{m\alpha}} and Δ~α​α\widetilde{\Delta}_{\alpha\alpha} parameters are taken from the Γ\Gamma-point energies [19], while the off-diagonal Δ−\Delta^{-} is fitted together with the other parameters. This procedure is a kind of approximation, because the energies at the Γ\Gamma point are already affected by the off-diagonal Δ−\Delta^{-} term [60].

It should be pointed out that, in the fitting procedure, a proper assignment of the E𝒌⋅𝒑E_{\bm{k}\cdot\bm{p}} bands to the DFT ones is crucial. As it is a known fact, the order of bands, classified by group representations, is not the same in all compounds. The identification of the bands in the Γ\Gamma point has been done with use of DFT tools (like projection of states on atomic orbitals, etc.), and the results are shown in Fig.1. It can be seen that there are 77 different cases of the band order, among which the most common is the one represented by GaAs.

Fitting procedures similar to the one described above have already been used by other authors, e.g. [61, 62], although there are some differences. In the cited works, a lower number of bands has been included in the 𝒌⋅𝒑\bm{k}\cdot\bm{p} (66 and 88) which allowed to apply a partly analytic form (the secular equation) and which caused the necessity of testing the values of the parameters as a function of the range of kk taken into account. We expect a good match in the whole BZ for the 3030-band 𝒌⋅𝒑\bm{k}\cdot\bm{p}, according to our previous experience, and thus, the kk-points range testing was not necessary and the points have been chosen arbitrarily. Also, a purely numerical diagonalization of the 𝒌⋅𝒑\bm{k}\cdot\bm{p} Hamiltonian has been applied for the fitting. We note that the fitting procedure, as well as the calculations described in the previous section, do not give reliable information about the signs of the parameters that enter the off-diagonal Hamiltonian blocks. Therefore, there is a some uncertainty about the signs of Pi{P}_{i}, Pi′{P}_{i}^{\prime} Qi{Q}_{i}, Ri{R}_{i} and Δ−\Delta^{-}, which is a drawback of our sets of parameters. We chose the most likely signs of the parameters not vanishing at the inversion symmetry by inspecting the wave functions obtained from the DFT. However, due to the uncertainty, we advise a caution in interpolation of the parameters for alloys.

VI Results and discussion

We begin the presentation and discussion of the results from GaAs, which is a well known III-V semiconductor. The 𝒌⋅𝒑\bm{k}\cdot\bm{p} parameters for this compound can be easily found in the literature [48, 63, 61, 64, 65, 66, 67]. However, most of the available parameters correspond to the 88 band 𝒌⋅𝒑\bm{k}\cdot\bm{p} model, derived from experiment (e.g. Ref. [64]), from a fitting to known band structures (e.g. Ref. [61]), or based on an extended literature review [48, 63]. In this work we present the parameters for the 3030 band 𝒌⋅𝒑\bm{k}\cdot\bm{p} model, whose advantage is an adequate representation of band structure in the whole BZ, as it has been shown in Ref. [19].

Figure 2 shows the GaAs band structures, the 3030-band 𝒌⋅𝒑\bm{k}\cdot\bm{p} one together with the DFT one used as a reference to find the k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p parameters. As it can be seen, the agreement is very satisfactory, particularly in 66 highest valence bands and 88 lowest conduction bands. This is a sufficient representation to model semiconductor devices, like LEDs, lasers, or solar cells. The respective parameters are given in the appropriate table later in the article.

The GaAs can be treated as a kind of a central compound among the III-V systems. In this work, we have calculated the k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p parameters for sixteen III-V semiconductor binary compounds, but we consider six compounds related to GaAs in order to have a look at the chemical trends, namely GaXX and YYAs, where YY and XX stand for the group III and V elements, respectively. The respective graphs are shown in Fig. 3. The overall view confirms the conclusion related to GaAs: the agreement between the DFT and the 3030-band 𝒌⋅𝒑\bm{k}\cdot\bm{p} band structures is good, particularly in the regions significant for the device modeling. The indirect gap is very well reproduced for GaP in GaXX as well as for BAs and AlAs in YYAs. This proves the reliability of the applied procedure. For the remaining nine compounds (the figures are in the attached Supplementary Material [41]), the electronic structure obtained by the DFT method is also well reconstructed using the 3030-band 𝒌⋅𝒑\bm{k}\cdot\bm{p} model.

The values of the k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p parameters for the sixteen III-V semiconductor compounds are listed in Tabs. 2-5. They can be directly used for physical phenomena analysis or in device modeling. As demonstrated in Appendix B, they could be also used for derivation of the standard parameters (the effective masses, the Luttinger parameters, etc.) for fewer-band models describing the vicinity of the Γ\Gamma point. However, it should be recalled that our parameters are optimized for the full BZ rather than for any specific 𝒌\bm{k} point. Therefore, more accurate parameters for the models with smaller number of bands could be obtained by a fitting in a narrower part of the BZ.

The chemical trends in the k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p parameters can be observed in Figs. 4(a-f), where the GaXX and YYAs values of the energies (a,b), the spin-orbit coupling parameters (c,d), and the parameters related to momentum matrix elements (e,f) are visualised. The GaXX (YYAs) compounds are ordered with respect to the atomic number of XX (YY). In many cases the behavior of parameters is monotonic and the variation is rather weak, but the chemical trends are clearly seen. For the energy parameters (a,b), it should be recalled that according to the applied convention the ab initio reference (zero) energy level is the top of the valence band.

In Figs. 4(a,b), the XX and YY element dependent values of the energy parameters can be seen. Since the E8​vE_{8\mathrm{v}} is set to zero as the reference energy, the parameter E5​vE_{5\mathrm{v}} is fixed to −Δv/3-\Delta_{\mathrm{v}}/3, which, in the energy scale of this plot, varies weakly with the atomic number. The behavior of the other parameters is rather systematic. Most of the conduction band energies decrease with the atomic number (of both XX and YY element). However, there are some exceptions, e.g. the E5​cE_{5\mathrm{c}} level in the YYAs dependence, where it is almost constant or slightly increasing. The lowest valence band level E1​wE_{1\mathrm{w}} increases, except to a slight decrease when changing from GaP to GaAs [Fig. 4(a)] and from AlAs to GaAs [Fig. 4(b)].

In Figs.4(c,d), the spin-orbit interaction parameters are shown. According to the adopted phase convention the Δ−\Delta^{-} is purely imaginary. For the XX element dependence [Fig.4(c)], the values of Δc\Delta_{\mathrm{c}}, Δd\Delta_{\mathrm{d}} do not change much (except the difference between GaN and GaP for Δc\Delta_{\mathrm{c}}). The strongest dependence is for the valence band parameter Δv\Delta_{\mathrm{v}}. It increases with the atomic number of XX and achieves the highest value of 0.7310.731 eV for GaSb. These values (Δv\Delta_{\mathrm{v}}) are in a good agreement with early predictions of Ref. [68]. Although, in the hydrogenic approximation, the spin-orbit interaction scales with the atomic number as ∝Z4\propto Z^{4}, it is known that this dependence is strongly suppressed by a screening [69]. In the case of YYAs [Fig.4(d)], one can observe a spectacularly increasing value of the Δc\Delta_{\mathrm{c}} parameter (except for the first two compounds), which in turn can be attributed to the increasing spin-orbit interaction in the YY element, whose orbitals contribute more to the conduction band. On the other hand, the increase of Δv\Delta_{\mathrm{v}} is much weaker (as compared to the GaXX dependence). The increase of the absolute value of Δ−\Delta^{-} from GaP to GaSb [Fig.4(c)] and its decrease from AlAs to InAs [Fig.4(d)] is consistent with the trends of the results in Ref. [70].

Finally, in Fig. 4(e,f), one can see the results for the parameters related to momentum matrix elements. An interesting observation is that their values, except for few cases, vary rather weakly. In this case, however, it is rather difficult to find a universal key explaining this behavior.

In Table. 6, we compare the values of P0​…​5P_{0...5}, P0,1′P^{\prime}_{0,1}, Q0,1Q_{0,1}, R0,1R_{0,1} parameters for GaAs, calculated from the fitting and extracted directly from the DFT (as described in Sec. IV and in Appendix C). We neglect the spin-orbit coupling in the determination of the DFT momentum matrix elements. Most of the fitted parameters are in a good agreement with the direct DFT approach. This shows that the effect of remote (not included in our k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p model) bands is relatively weak. The differences get larger only for smaller parameters, like P1P_{1} and P0′P_{0}^{\prime}.

There are also some, although limited, reference data in the literature. A comparison of the parameters evaluated in this work and those found in the literature (Refs. [9, 71, 72, 73]) for GaAs, InP, InAs, InSb, AlAs and GaP is made in Tab.7. One should note that different references could adopt various phase conventions. Therefore, to facilitate a comparison, we use the absolute values of Δ−\Delta^{-} and also EM=2​m0ℏ2​|M|2E_{M}=\frac{2m_{0}}{\hbar^{2}}\absolutevalue{M}^{2}, where MM are the parameters related to interband momentum matrix elements. The energy parameters in Tab.7 are given in the double-group notation, where

E6​α\displaystyle E_{6\alpha} =E1​α,\displaystyle=E_{1\alpha},
E8​α\displaystyle E_{8\alpha} =E5​α+13​Δα,\displaystyle=E_{5\alpha}+\frac{1}{3}\Delta_{\alpha},
E7​α\displaystyle E_{7\alpha} =E5​α−23​Δα,\displaystyle=E_{5\alpha}-\frac{2}{3}\Delta_{\alpha},

with except to α=\alpha=’’t‘‘ where E8​t=E3​tE_{8\mathrm{t}}=E_{3\mathrm{t}}. In most cases, the discrepancies of our results and the literature data are reasonable. Here however, we offer the parameters for all the 1616 compounds, obtained in a consistent way.

For many III-V compounds with a direct band gap, the 88-band 𝒌⋅𝒑\bm{k}\cdot\bm{p} model is sufficient because the description of the electronic band structure around the Γ\Gamma point of the BZ is good enough. Therefore, the 3030-band 𝒌⋅𝒑\bm{k}\cdot\bm{p} model is rarely used for GaAs, GaSb, InP, InAs and InSb, but it is already necessary for III-V compounds with an indirect band gap (BXX, AlXX, and GaP) in order to describe the side valleys correctly. The BXX compounds are experimentally the least studied ones, and the k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p parameters for these compounds have not been reported so far.

The electronic band structures for BXX compounds were calculated by DFT methods and reported in many articles [74, 75, 76, 77, 78], but experimental studies of the band gap for cubic BXX are limited to a few cases [79, 80, 81, 82, 83, 84, 85], mostly for BAs. The interest in BAs increased suddenly in 2013 when DFT calculations predicted BAs as a highly thermal conductive material with a thermal conductivity comparable with that of diamond [86, 87]. Subsequent intense research led to a successful synthesis and verification of the predicted high thermal conductive material in 2018 by three groups [88, 89, 90], opening up new opportunities for both basic research and potential applications. A very important application of BXX compounds can be their alloying with the GaAs, InAs, and other III-V compounds. This aspect is interesting as it allows a wider range of strain engineering for some III-V alloys, especially GaAs-based semiconductors [20].

VII Examples of application

The optical gain for bulk materials was calculated as an exemplary application to highlight the importance of choice of the band model. The calculations were conducted for GaAs and GaSb using the 3030-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p and the 88-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p models. Details regarding the calculation of the gain for these models are in the work [19]. Here we calculate the 𝒌\bm{k}-dependent momentum matrix elements, using the Hellmann-Feynman theorem[91, 92, 93]

P~n,i​j​(𝒌)≈m0ℏ​∂Hi​j​(𝒌)∂kn,\widetilde{P}_{n,ij}(\bm{k})\approx\frac{m_{0}}{\hbar}\partialderivative{H_{ij}(\kk)}{k_n},

where Hi​jH_{ij} are the matrix elements of the 88- or 3030-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p Hamiltonian. The parameters needed for calculations within the 8-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p model: the effective mass and the Luttinger parameters were taken from the transformations presented in Appendix B (the reduced parameters denoted as m′m^{\prime} and γ1−3′\gamma^{\prime}_{1-3}). Our objective was to perform calculations that will refer to the same band structure. Therefore, the calculations were performed with the parameters from Appendix B, despite the fact that for some materials they are inaccurate. The gain for both materials was calculated in the same range of carrier concentration from 1.0⋅1018​cm−31.0\cdot 10^{18}\mathrm{cm}^{-3} to 1.0⋅1019​cm−31.0\cdot 10^{19}\mathrm{cm}^{-3}. The calculations were made for a temperature of 300300 K. The position of the conduction bands was shifted by 8080 meV in order to take the influence of temperature into account. The calculations made within the two models give very similar results for GaAs. We can notice a difference in the intensity of the calculated gain coefficient. However, the shape of the spectrum and the maximum gain is almost the same. These differences become particularly noticeable for greater concentrations. This is due to the lack of consideration of the influence of the side valleys in the 8-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p model. The situation is quite different for GaSb. The presented gain spectrum shows the legitimacy of using the larger-band model for gain calculations. The L valley is located very close to the Γ\Gamma valley in GaSb material. Therefore, the influence of the side valley is already visible for lower concentrations and practically should be taken into account in order to obtain correct results. It is also clear that, for semiconductors with an indirect energy gap, it is necessary to take into account the contribution of the side valleys for the calculation of the gain. This can be done by using the 30-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p model because this model can satisfactory reflect the band structure of such materials.

VIII Conclusions

We have derived a ready-to-use symmetry invariant expansion of the 3030-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p Hamiltonian. We have obtained its parameters for a wide class of III-V semiconductor compounds using the DFT band structure calculations as a reference. We have demonstrated a very good agreement between the DFT and the k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p results. We have also discussed the chemical trends exhibited by the parameters. Finally, for GaAs, we have also compared the parameters obtained from the fitting and calculated directly from the DFT momentum matrix elements. We have shown a very good agreement for most of these values.

Appendix A Supplemental description and a derivation of the 30-band 𝒌⋅𝒑\bm{k}\!\dotproduct\!\bm{p} Hamiltonian in the invariant expansion

In this Appendix, we describe the standard theory of invariants for the k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p model [42, 33]. Then, we use this approach to obtain an invariant expansion of the 3030-band Hamiltonian.

A general form of the k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p model is given by [33]

H=H0+Hk+Hk⋅p+Hso,H=H_{0}+H_{k}+H_{k\!\dotproduct\!p}+H_{\mathrm{so}}, (3)

where

H0\displaystyle H_{0} =ℏ22​m0​p2+V⁡(𝒓),\displaystyle=\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m_{0}}p^{2}+V(\bm{r}),
Hk\displaystyle H_{k} =ℏ22​m0​k2,\displaystyle=\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m_{0}}k^{2},
Hk⋅p\displaystyle H_{k\!\dotproduct\!p} =ℏm0​𝒌⋅𝒑,\displaystyle=\frac{\hbar}{m_{0}}\bm{k}\cdot\bm{p},
Hso\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{so}} =ℏ4​m02​c2(∇V×𝒑)⋅𝝈,\displaystyle=\frac{\hbar}{4m^{2}_{0}c^{2}}(\nabla V\times\bm{p})\cdot\bm{\sigma},

where m0m_{0} is the free electron mass, V⁡(𝒓)V(\bm{r}) is a periodic crystal potential, cc is the speed of light, and 𝝈\bm{\sigma} is the vector of the Pauli matrices. Here, the spin-orbital terms proportional simultaneously to 𝒌\bm{k} and ∇V\nabla V are neglected.

In a truncated (finite) basis, the Hamiltonian takes a matrix form. For the 3030-band model considered in this paper, we use the set of basis functions from Ref. 9, transformed to the form consistent with Ref. [38]

|𝚪6​q⟩\displaystyle\ket{\bm{\Gamma}_{6\mathrm{q}}} ={|Sq⟩⊗|↑⟩,|Sq⟩⊗|↓⟩,\displaystyle=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\ket{S_\mathrm{q}}\otimes\ket{\uparrow},\\[4.0pt] \ket{S_\mathrm{q}}\otimes\ket{\downarrow},\end{array}\right.
|𝚪8​d⟩\displaystyle\ket{\bm{\Gamma}_{8\mathrm{d}}} ={−12|Xd+i​Yd⟩⊗|↑⟩,26​|Zd⟩⊗|↑⟩−16​|Xd+i​Yd⟩⊗|↓⟩,16​|Xd−i​Yd⟩⊗|↑⟩+26​|Zd⟩⊗|↓⟩,12​|Xd−i​Yd⟩⊗|↓⟩,\displaystyle=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{X_\mathrm{d}+iY_\mathrm{d}}\otimes\ket{\uparrow},\\[4.0pt] \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\ket{Z_\mathrm{d}}\otimes\ket{\uparrow}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\ket{X_\mathrm{d}+iY_\mathrm{d}}\otimes\ket{\downarrow},\\[4.0pt] \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\ket{X_\mathrm{d}-iY_\mathrm{d}}\otimes\ket{\uparrow}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\ket{Z_\mathrm{d}}\otimes\ket{\downarrow},\\[4.0pt] \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{X_\mathrm{d}-iY_\mathrm{d}}\otimes\ket{\downarrow},\end{array}\right.

|𝚪7​v⟩\displaystyle\ket{\bm{\Gamma}_{7\mathrm{v}}} ={−13|Zv⟩⊗|↑⟩−13|Xv+i​Yv⟩⊗|↓⟩,−13|Xv−i​Yv⟩⊗|↑⟩+13|Zv⟩⊗|↓⟩,\displaystyle=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\ket{Z_\mathrm{v}}\otimes\ket{\uparrow}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\ket{X_\mathrm{v}+iY_\mathrm{v}}\otimes\ket{\downarrow},\\[4.0pt] -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\ket{X_\mathrm{v}-iY_\mathrm{v}}\otimes\ket{\uparrow}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\ket{Z_\mathrm{v}}\otimes\ket{\downarrow},\\[4.0pt] \end{array}\right.

where |S⟩\ket{S}, |X⟩\ket{X}, |Y⟩\ket{Y}, |Z⟩\ket{Z}, |D1⟩=|2​Z2−X2−Y2⟩\ket{D_1}=\ket{2Z^2-X^2-Y^2}, |D2⟩=|3​(X2−Y2)⟩\ket{D_{2}}=\ket{\sqrt{3}\qty(X^2-Y^2)} describe the orbital symmetry, while |↑/↓⟩\ket{\uparrow/\downarrow} denotes the spin projection. where vq(1)v^{(1)}_{q} are the spherical vector components (with the upper index as the tensor rank) defined with respect to the cartesian ones in the standard way:

v0(1)\displaystyle v^{(1)}_{0} =vz,\displaystyle=v_{z},
v1(1)\displaystyle v^{(1)}_{1} =−12​(vx+i​vy).\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\quantity(v_x + i v_y).

The vector X(1)X^{(1)} can be calculated using tensor multiplication rules giving

(4)

where we show the order of bands relevant for most of the considered III-V semiconductors (like in GaAs). The block positions can be related to fewer-band models that are often used in the semiconductor physics. The part of Eq.4 which is highlighted by the blue color (H6​c​6​cH_{\mathrm{6c6c}}) describes the lowest conduction band and corresponds to the 22-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p Hamiltonian [35]. The part marked by the red color contains the highest valence band block H8​v​8​vH_{\mathrm{8v8v}} describing the heavy and light hole, and the spin-orbit split-off bands H7​v​7​vH_{\mathrm{7v7v}}. The part separated by the solid line corresponds to the standard 88-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p model [95], while the gray area extends the model to 1414 bands [32, 38]. One should recall, that reduction of the full 3030-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p model to a model with fewer number of bands involves a perturbative approach, as described in Appendix B.

The invariant expansion of the 30-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p Hamiltonian can be written in an explicit form

H6​q​6​q\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{6q6q}} =(E1​q+ℏ22​m0​k2)​𝕀2,\displaystyle=\quantity( E_{\mathrm{1q}} + \frac{\hbar^2}{2m_0} k^2 )\;\mathbb{I}_{2},
H8​d​8​d\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{8d8d}} =(E5​d+13​Δd+ℏ22​m0​k2)​𝕀4,\displaystyle=\quantity( E_{\mathrm{5d}} + \frac{1}{3} \Delta_{\mathrm{d}} + \frac{\hbar^2}{2m_0} k^2 )\;\mathbb{I}_{4},
H7​d​7​d\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{7d7d}} =(E5​d−23​Δd+ℏ22​m0​k2)​𝕀2,\displaystyle=\quantity( E_{\mathrm{5d}} - \frac{2}{3} \Delta_{\mathrm{d}} + \frac{\hbar^2}{2m_0} k^2 )\;\mathbb{I}_{2},
H8​t​8​t\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{8t8t}} =(E3​t+ℏ22​m0​k2)​𝕀4,\displaystyle=\quantity( E_{\mathrm{3t}} + \frac{\hbar^2}{2m_0} k^2 )\;\mathbb{I}_{4},
H6​u​6​u\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{6u6u}} =(E1​u+ℏ22​m0​k2)​𝕀2,\displaystyle=\quantity( E_{\mathrm{1u}} + \frac{\hbar^2}{2m_0} k^2 )\;\mathbb{I}_{2},
H8​c​8​c\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{8c8c}} =(E5​c+13​Δc+ℏ22​m0​k2)​𝕀4,\displaystyle=\quantity( E_{\mathrm{5c}} + \frac{1}{3} \Delta_{\mathrm{c}} + \frac{\hbar^2}{2m_0} k^2 )\;\mathbb{I}_{4},
H7​c​7​c\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{7c7c}} =(E5​c−23​Δc+ℏ22​m0​k2)​𝕀2,\displaystyle=\quantity( E_{\mathrm{5c}} - \frac{2}{3} \Delta_{\mathrm{c}} + \frac{\hbar^2}{2m_0} k^2 )\;\mathbb{I}_{2},
H6​c​6​c\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{6c6c}} =(E1​c+ℏ22​m0​k2)​𝕀2,\displaystyle=\quantity( E_{\mathrm{1c}} + \frac{\hbar^2}{2m_0} k^2 )\;\mathbb{I}_{2},
H8​v​8​v\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{8v8v}} =(E5​v+13​Δv+ℏ22​m0​k2)​𝕀4,\displaystyle=\quantity( E_{\mathrm{5v}} + \frac{1}{3} \Delta_{\mathrm{v}} + \frac{\hbar^2}{2m_0} k^2 )\;\mathbb{I}_{4},
H7​v​7​v\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{7v7v}} =(E5​v−23​Δv+ℏ22​m0​k2)​𝕀2,\displaystyle=\quantity( E_{\mathrm{5v}} - \frac{2}{3} \Delta_{\mathrm{v}} + \frac{\hbar^2}{2m_0} k^2 )\;\mathbb{I}_{2},
H6​w​6​w\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{6w6w}} =(E1​w+ℏ22​m0​k2)​𝕀2,\displaystyle=\quantity( E_{\mathrm{1w}} + \frac{\hbar^2}{2m_0} k^2 )\;\mathbb{I}_{2},
H6​q​8​d\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{6q8d}} =3​P3​(Tx​kx+c.p.),\displaystyle=\sqrt{3}P_{3}\quantity(T_x k_x + \cp),
H6​q​7​d\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{6q7d}} =−13​P3​(σx​kx+c.p.),\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}P_{3}\quantity(\sigma_x k_x + \cp),
H6​q​8​v\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{6q8v}} =3P2(Txkx+c.p.),\displaystyle=\sqrt{3}P_{2}(T_{x}k_{x}+{\mathrm{c.p.}}),
H6​q​7​v\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{6q7v}} =−13P2(σxkx+c.p.),\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}P_{2}(\sigma_{x}k_{x}+{\mathrm{c.p.}}),
H8​d​8​t\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{8d8t}} =−30R1(Dx†kx+c.p.),\displaystyle=-\sqrt{30}\ R_{1}(D^{\dagger}_{x}k_{x}+{\mathrm{c.p.}}),
H8​d​8​c\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{8d8c}} =−23​Q1​({Jy,Jz}​kx+c.p.),\displaystyle=-\frac{2}{3}Q_{1}\quantity(\{J_y,J_z\} k_x + \cp),
H8​d​7​c\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{8d7c}} =−2Q1(Ty​z†kx+c.p.),\displaystyle=-2Q_{1}(T^{\dagger}_{yz}k_{x}+{\mathrm{c.p.}}),
H8​d​6​c\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{8d6c}} =3P1(Tx†kx+c.p.),\displaystyle=\sqrt{3}P_{1}(T^{\dagger}_{x}k_{x}+{\mathrm{c.p.}}),
H7​d​8​t\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{7d8t}} =6​R1​(Tx​kx+c.p.),\displaystyle=\sqrt{6}R_{1}\quantity(T_x k_x+\cp),

Table 8 contains the optical energy parameter (EP0=2​m0ℏ2​|P0|2E_{\mathrm{P_{0}}}=\frac{2m_{0}}{\hbar^{2}}|P_{0}|^{2}), the Luttinger parameters (γ1\gamma_{1}, γ2\gamma_{2}, and γ3\gamma_{3}), and the electron effective mass (m∗m^{*}) for Γ6​c\Gamma_{6c}, for all the considered binary compounds. They were calculated using Eqs. 5–8 with the parameters listed in Tables 2-5.

Table 9 contains: the lattice parameters (alca_{\mathrm{lc}}); the direct energy gaps at the Γ\Gamma point (EgΓE_{\mathrm{g}}^{\Gamma}); the indirect energy gaps to the Δ\Delta and Λ\Lambda valleys (EgΔE_{\mathrm{g}}^{\Delta} and EgΛE_{\mathrm{g}}^{\Lambda}); the spin-orbit splittings of the top valence bands (Δso\Delta_{\mathrm{so}}); the effective masses in the first conduction band at the Γ\Gamma point (mem_{\mathrm{e}}); the absolute values of the effective masses of heavy holes and light holes along three crystallographic directions (|mhh100||m_{\mathrm{hh}}^{100}|, |mhh110||m_{\mathrm{hh}}^{110}|, |mhh111||m_{\mathrm{hh}}^{111}|, |mlh100||m_{\mathrm{lh}}^{100}|, |mlh110||m_{\mathrm{lh}}^{110}|, and |mlh111||m_{\mathrm{lh}}^{111}|); the effective masses in the split-off band at the Γ\Gamma point (msom_{\mathrm{so}}); and the longitudinal effective masses in the Δ\Delta- and LL-valleys (mΔm_{\Delta} and mLm_{L}). All the lattice parameters are obtained as described in Sec. III. The remaining parameters are obtained numerically from the electronic-band structures computed within the 30-band k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p with the parameters listed in Tables 2-5. We note that Δso\Delta_{\mathrm{so}} are slightly different compared to the Δv\Delta_{\mathrm{v}} parameters presented in the main text. The reason is the influence of the off-diagonal spin-orbit coupling terms with parameter Δ−\Delta^{-} which shifts the bands [60]. While for most of the compounds its influence is negligible, in some cases (like BSb), the Δso\Delta_{\mathrm{so}} differs to the value of Δv\Delta_{\mathrm{v}} by a few percent.

Effective masses at the Γ\Gamma point and at the minima of the Δ\Delta- and LL-valleys are evaluated with use of the standard formula

mni​j​k=[m0ℏ2​∂2En∂ki​j​k2]−1,\displaystyle m_{n}^{ijk}=\left[\frac{m_{0}}{\hbar^{2}}\frac{\partial^{2}E_{n}}{\partial k_{ijk}^{2}}\right]^{-1},

where i​j​kijk denotes chosen crystallographic direction and nn is a label of a given band.

Appendix C Interband momentum matrix elements from the DFT

In this part, we describe a method to extract the k⋅pk\!\dotproduct\!p parameters directly from the DFT momentum matrix elements. The calculations were performed without the spin-orbit coupling. Although we worked with a reduced basis neglecting spin (15 states) in the numerical calculations, we present a derivation of the parameters with the full basis that includes spin (30 states) for the sake of consistency with the main part of the paper.

The bare interband parameters are given with respect to the basis states (with modified and combined notations of Refs. [38, 9]) as

𝒫a​b\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{ab} =ℏm0​⟨Sa|p^x|Xb⟩,\displaystyle=\frac{\hbar}{m_{0}}\matrixelement{S_a}{\hat{p}_x}{X_b},
𝒬a​b\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{ab} =ℏm0​⟨Xa|p^y|Zb⟩,\displaystyle=\frac{\hbar}{m_{0}}\matrixelement{X_a}{\hat{p}_y}{Z_b},
ℛt​b\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{t}b} =ℏm0​⟨Dt,1|p^x|Xb⟩\displaystyle=\frac{\hbar}{m_{0}}\matrixelement{D_{\mathrm{t},1}}{\hat{p}_x}{X_b}
=−13​ℏm0​⟨Dt,2|p^x|Xb⟩,\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\frac{\hbar}{m_{0}}\matrixelement{D_{\mathrm{t},2}}{\hat{p}_x}{X_b},

where a,ba,b label the band sets: ’’w”, ’’v”, ’’c”, ’’u”, ’’d”, ’’q” (except to ’’t”). To obtain the value of P0≡𝒫cv=ℏm0​⟨Sc|p^x|Xv⟩P_{0}\equiv\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{c}\mathrm{v}}=\frac{\hbar}{m_{0}}\matrixelement{S_\mathrm{c}}{\hat{p}_x}{X_\mathrm{v}} directly from the DFT, one need to calculate the elements (px)n​m=⟨Ψn(c)|p^x|Ψm(v)⟩(p_{x})_{nm}=\matrixelement{\Psi^\mathrm{(c)}_n}{\hat{p}_{x}}{\Psi^\mathrm{(v)}_m} between the states from the twofold degenerated conduction band ’’6c” and the sixfold degenerated valence band ’’8v ⊕\oplus 7v” (as the spin-orbit coupling is neglected here). Hence the relevant block (px)n​m(p_{x})_{nm} is 2×62\times 6. The states can be further expressed as

|Ψn(c)⟩\displaystyle\ket{\Psi^\mathrm{(c)}_n} =∑σ=↑,↓ασ(n)​|Sc⟩⊗|σ⟩,\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma=\uparrow,\downarrow}\alpha^{(n)}_{\sigma}\ket{ S_\mathrm{c}}\otimes\ket{\sigma},
|Ψm(v)⟩\displaystyle\ket{\Psi^\mathrm{(v)}_m} =∑σ=↑,↓∑i=x,y,zβi​σ(m)​|rv,i⟩⊗|σ⟩,\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma=\uparrow,\downarrow}\sum_{i=x,y,z}\beta^{(m)}_{i\sigma}\ket{r_{\mathrm{v},i}}\otimes\ket{\sigma},

where ασ(n)\alpha^{(n)}_{\sigma}, βi​σ(m)\beta^{(m)}_{i\sigma} are complex coefficients, σ\sigma denotes spin, and we use the notation |rv,x⟩≡|Xv⟩\ket{r_{\mathrm{v},x}}\equiv\ket{X_{\mathrm{v}}}, |rv,y⟩≡|Yv⟩\ket{r_{\mathrm{v},y}}\equiv\ket{Y_{\mathrm{v}}}, |rv,z⟩≡|Zv⟩\ket{r_{\mathrm{v},z}}\equiv\ket{Z_{\mathrm{v}}}. The substitution leads to

(px)n​m=∑σ=↑,↓∑i=x,y,zασ(n)∗βi​σ(m)⟨Sc|p^x|rv,i⟩.(p_{x})_{nm}=\sum_{\sigma=\uparrow,\downarrow}\sum_{i=x,y,z}\alpha^{(n)*}_{\sigma}\beta^{(m)}_{i\sigma}\matrixelement{S_\mathrm{c}}{\hat{p}_x}{r_{\mathrm{v},i}}.

Taking a sum over the moduli square, one can obtain

∑n,m|(px)n​m|2=∑σ=↑,↓∑i=x,y,z|⟨Sc|p^x|rv,i⟩|2.\sum_{n,m}\absolutevalue{(p_{x})_{nm} }^{2}=\sum_{\sigma=\uparrow,\downarrow}\sum_{i=x,y,z}\absolutevalue{ \mel{S_\mathrm{c}}{\hat{p}_x}{r_{\mathrm{v},i}}}^{2}.

Since ⟨Sc|p^x|rv,i⟩=m0ℏ​P0​δx​i\matrixelement{S_\mathrm{c}}{\hat{p}_x}{r_{\mathrm{v},i}}=\frac{m_{0}}{\hbar}P_{0}\,\delta_{xi} and it does not depend on spin, one can get

|P0|=ℏm0​12​∑n,m|(px)n​m|2.\absolutevalue{P_0}=\frac{\hbar}{m_{0}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n,m}\absolutevalue{(p_{x})_{nm} }^{2}}.

In the same way, one can find the other elements of the 𝒫a​b\mathcal{P}_{ab} type.

To calculate Q0≡𝒬cv=ℏm0​⟨Xc|p^y|Zv⟩Q_{0}\equiv\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{c}\mathrm{v}}=\frac{\hbar}{m_{0}}\matrixelement{X_\mathrm{c}}{\hat{p}_y}{Z_\mathrm{v}} we take

(py)n​m=∑σ∑i,jβi​σ(n)∗βj​σ(m)⟨rc,i|p^y|rv,j⟩,(p_{y})_{nm}=\sum_{\sigma}\sum_{i,j}\beta^{(n)*}_{i\sigma}\beta^{(m)}_{j\sigma}\matrixelement{r_{\mathrm{c},i}}{\hat{p}_y}{r_{\mathrm{v},j}},

where the block (py)n​m(p_{y})_{nm} is 6×66\times 6 now. In the next step, one can obtain

∑n,m|(py)n​m|2=2​∑i,j|⟨rc,i|p^y|rv,j⟩|2,\sum_{n,m}\absolutevalue{(p_{y})_{nm} }^{2}=2\sum_{i,j}\absolutevalue{ \mel{r_{\mathrm{c},i}}{\hat{p}_y}{r_{\mathrm{v},j}}}^{2},

where the factor of 2 results from the summation over spin projections. Since |⟨Xc|p^y|Zv⟩|2=|⟨Zc|p^y|Xv⟩|2=m02ℏ2​|Q0|2\absolutevalue{\mel{X_\mathrm{c}}{\hat{p}_y}{Z_\mathrm{v}}}^{2}=\absolutevalue{\mel{Z_\mathrm{c}}{\hat{p}_y}{X_\mathrm{v}}}^{2}=\frac{m^{2}_{0}}{\hbar^{2}}\absolutevalue{Q_0}^{2}, one can get

|Q0|=ℏ2​m0​∑n,m|(py)n​m|2.\absolutevalue{Q_0}=\frac{\hbar}{2m_{0}}\sqrt{\sum_{n,m}\absolutevalue{(p_{y})_{nm} }^{2}}.

The parameter Q1Q_{1} is calculated analogously.

In the case of R0=ℛtvR_{0}=\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{t}\mathrm{v}}, using (px)n​m=⟨Ψn(t)|p^x|Ψm(v)⟩(p_{x})_{nm}=\matrixelement{\Psi^\mathrm{(t)}_n}{\hat{p}_{x}}{\Psi^\mathrm{(v)}_m}, one needs to express

|Ψn(t)⟩\displaystyle\ket{\Psi^\mathrm{(t)}_n} =∑σ=↑,↓∑i=12γi,σ(n)​|Dt,i⟩⊗|σ⟩,\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma=\uparrow,\downarrow}\sum_{i=1}^{2}\gamma^{(n)}_{i,\sigma}\ket{D_{\mathrm{t},i}}\otimes\ket{\sigma},

giving

∑n,m|(px)n​m|2=2​∑i=12∑j=x,y,z|⟨Dt,i|p^x|rv,j⟩|2.\sum_{n,m}\absolutevalue{(p_{x})_{nm} }^{2}=2\sum_{i=1}^{2}\sum_{j=x,y,z}\absolutevalue{ \mel{D_{\mathrm{t},i}}{\hat{p}_x}{r_{\mathrm{v},j}}}^{2}.

The non-zero contributions at the right-hand side come from ⟨Dt,1|p^x|Xv⟩=m0ℏ​R0\matrixelement{D_{\mathrm{t},1}}{\hat{p}_x}{X_{\mathrm{v}}}=\frac{m_{0}}{\hbar}R_{0} and ⟨Dt,2|p^x|Xv⟩=−3​m0ℏ​R0\matrixelement{D_{\mathrm{t},2}}{\hat{p}_x}{X_{\mathrm{v}}}=-\sqrt{3}\frac{m_{0}}{\hbar}R_{0}. Therefore

|R0|=ℏm0​18​∑n,m|(px)n​m|2.\absolutevalue{R_0}=\frac{\hbar}{m_{0}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{8}\sum_{n,m}\absolutevalue{(p_{x})_{nm} }^{2}}.

The parameter R1R_{1} can be obtained analogously.
